definition.text: Soil in cities and towns, often stripped of its topsoil, compacted and contaminated by human activity.

facts.text: Urban soil holds more heavy metals, especially lead, copper and nickel, and has a lower pH than comparable soil in the wild.
With the topsoil typically stripped away, it has low aeration, porosity and drainage; compaction and contamination limit root growth and tree health.
Contamination persists in cities with a history of industry, leaded gasoline or lead-based house paint.
The Polish soil classification's 'urban soils' type corresponds to Urbic, Mollic or Ecranic Technosols in the WRB.
Urban soil management is interdisciplinary, aiming to protect soil biodiversity, cut industrial pollution and make soils more resilient to construction compaction.
In a Palermo trial, de-sealing long-sealed urban soils and revegetating them stabilised infiltration and raised microbial activity within eighteen months.
Construction rather than farm machinery is the usual cause of urban compaction: jobs on tight schedules ignore the risk of working wet soil, and topsoil is stripped or fill added.
Disturbed urban soils are low in organic matter and biological activity, and construction debris such as concrete often raises the pH because concrete contains lime.

definition.text: Objects in soil recognizably made or extracted from the earth by humans, a defining feature of human-made soils.

facts.text: A significant amount of artefacts, a geotechnical liner or a seal of technic hard material qualifies a soil as a Technosol.
The WRB uses the horizon suffix τ for human-transported natural material.
Dark earth may contain fragments of pottery, tile, animal bone and other artefacts.

definition.text: A designed planted site, also called a bioretention facility, that lets runoff from roofs, roads and other hard urban surfaces soak into the soil and be cleaned.

facts.text: Plants and natural or engineered soil hold stormwater, delay infiltration, and filter and remediate pollutants carried by urban runoff.
Deep roots open extra channels for infiltration, maintain soil permeability and sustain the microbes that break down pollutants and remove nitrogen.
Water is cleaned by settling, filtration, assimilation, adsorption to roots, soil particles and organic matter, and microbial decomposition.
Typical removal is about 80% of suspended solids and 50–60% of heavy metals; a 2025 meta-analysis found loads of nitrogen and phosphorus cut by about 55% and 62%.
They restore groundwater recharge and cut stormwater volumes, but may not reduce pollution unless remediation materials are built into the filter layers.

definition.text: The engineered growing soil, or substrate, through which a rain garden filters collected water.

facts.text: A typical mix is 60% sand, 20% compost and 20% topsoil; more compost improves filtering, while more sand improves infiltration but may retain fewer nutrients.
The sandy mix must not be blended with less sandy surrounding soil, since clay settles between sand grains into a concrete-like, poorly draining mass.
Where native soil drains too slowly, such as Type D soils, it should be replaced and an underdrain installed.
A five-year USGS study found rain gardens in urban clay soils worked without underdrains or soil replacement if pre-installation infiltration was at least 0.25 in/hour.

definition.text: A pile of topsoil excavated during construction of buildings or infrastructure and kept for later use.

facts.text: The soil is stored for later landscaping or restoration once construction infrastructure is removed, making it a resource for both construction and ecology.
Before re-use, stockpiled soil may be tested for contamination.

definition.text: A pile of spoil, the waste earth material removed during mining or large excavations.

facts.text: Spoil may be ordinary soil and rock or heavily contaminated with chemical waste; clean spoil can be used for land reclamation.
Tips trap solar heat, hindering plant establishment and encouraging erosion and unstable slopes; they also cause acid rock drainage and leach noxious chemicals into groundwater.
In 1966 a tip at Aberfan, Wales, built over a spring and saturated by heavy rain, collapsed onto a school, killing 144 people.
Regreening uses geotextiles to control erosion while the site is resoiled and seeded; old tips may later shelter rare plants, though without nearby seed sources invasive species dominate.

definition.text: The care and management of single trees and tree populations in towns and cities to improve the urban environment.

facts.text: Trees aid stormwater management by intercepting rain in the canopy and slowing, filtering and returning water to the air through their roots.
Street trees face limited soil volume, high soil compaction and harsh microclimates, so they grow and survive less well than trees elsewhere.
Species are chosen for tolerance of alkaline and compacted soils, low soil volume, de-icing salts and drought; healthy large trees need about 1,000 cubic feet of soil.
Urban forests support services such as nutrient cycling and soil formation.

definition.text: Contamination is much more prevalent in urban soils than agricultural ones, lead being the most common contaminant.

facts.text: Lead is widespread because of its long use in gasoline (banned in the US since 1989) and paint (banned for residential use since 1978); other contaminants include petroleum products and legacy pesticides such as lead arsenate and copper sulfate.
Of special concern are former industrial sites, roadsides, recent construction sites, waste disposal sites and junkyards; contaminants can also arrive by atmospheric deposition.
People are exposed by ingesting soil, breathing dust and volatiles, eating crops, and through skin; risk is greatest on bare soil and for children.
Plants absorb little lead, especially at neutral pH, so dirty hands, dust and unwashed produce are the larger exposure; lead can accumulate in roots, so root crops should be avoided.
Solvents such as trichloroethylene move readily to groundwater, some pesticides persist for years, and petroleum products tend to stay near the surface where they can be scraped off.
Road salt (sodium chloride) causes sodic conditions, aggregate breakdown and compaction.

definition.text: Assessing an urban site starts with researching its past use before any soil is sampled.

facts.text: Land-use history comes from owners, old aerial photos, maps, permits and tax records, plus a visit to look for sources such as peeling lead paint or a nearby highway; green-space or residential histories usually mean fewer problems than industrial ones.
There are no federal contaminant limits in the US for gardens; the EPA recommends testing for pH, organic matter, nutrients, micronutrients and metals including lead.

Samples may be needed per contaminant and at different depths (metals near the surface, solvents deeper), and because distribution is unpredictable many locations and suspect spots near old buildings, bare patches or drains need separate sampling.
Lead rarely harms plants, but copper, zinc and nickel can be phytotoxic at high concentrations.
A full assessment also considers slope, drainage and buried utility lines.

definition.text: Reconditioning improves degraded urban soil with physical, chemical and biological practices, generally applied in that order.

facts.text: Removing contaminated soil by excavation is expensive and regulated; if contamination is modest or shallow, scraping the surface and replacing it with good topsoil is more feasible.
Tillage or subsoiling can dilute a thin contaminated layer into deeper soil and relieve compaction; where compaction is the main problem, amelioration in place is better than removal.
Phosphorus binds lead and makes it less dangerous over time; lime or dolomite can stabilize pH.
Compost and other organic amendments raise organic matter, improve structure and biology, dilute toxic compounds and bind some contaminants, but the compost itself must be free of contaminants.
Mulch suppresses weeds, reduces erosion and splash, and acts as a barrier to contact with contaminated soil.

definition.text: Green spaces need soil with good drainage, high water-holding capacity and good rooting at low maintenance cost.

facts.text: Except in extreme contamination, poor soil can be buried under trucked-in topsoil or improved with amendments; burying in place often suffices for built sites with debris.
Raised beds or berms address poor soil and drainage; landscape fabric under imported soil limits roots reaching the original soil.
The scoop-and-dump method mixes compost into compacted soil with excavators, and an air spader blows compacted soil from around roots of trees to be saved.

title: Container and green roof soil mixes

definition.text: Pots, planters and green roofs need clean, light soil mixes with excellent drainage and high water- and nutrient-holding capacity.

facts.text: Rooftop mixes must be light enough not to overload the roof yet heavy enough to anchor plants against wind and water.
Mixes combine heat-treated vermiculite and perlite with organic materials such as peat moss, compost or biochar; they are low in density but cost more than ordinary soil.

definition.text: Gap-graded soil contains only certain particle sizes, with some sizes left out deliberately to guarantee pore space.

facts.text: Street trees face a dilemma: pavement needs a compacted substrate to bear loads, while roots need a healthy rooting environment, and trees often die early from constricted roots, salt, heat and moisture stress.
Large uniform stones form a load-bearing skeleton while the large pores, partly filled with high-quality soil, let roots grow under the pavement.
Golf greens use similar gap-graded sand to support foot traffic while keeping turf healthy.

definition.text: Good construction practice limits traffic and protects topsoil to avoid lasting compaction and mixing of soil layers.

facts.text: Digging for pipes or drains mixes fertile topsoil with subsoil, leaving poor soil at the surface; compaction matters little under pavement but long-term where land is revegetated.
Controlled traffic lanes, metal plates or geotextile under gravel, and avoiding work on wet soil limit compaction.
Strip and stockpile topsoil separately, refill subsoil first and loosen it with rippers, then replace topsoil without further compaction.
